title: The Letter to the Philippians
subtitle: Pros Philippēsious, “To the Philippians”
description: Paul’s warmest letter, written in chains to the first church he founded in Europe, the friends at Philippi who had stood by him from the first day and had just sent him a gift. He does not know whether he will live or die, and finds that either is good: “For me, living is Christ, and dying is gain.” A plea for unity built on the great passage of Christ who emptied himself and took on the form of a servant; Paul counting all his advantages as loss to gain Christ, and running for the prize; two quarrelling friends urged to agree; and joy, prayer, peace and the secret of contentment: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Philippians?
qa.answer: The eleventh book of the New Testament, a short letter of the apostle Paul to the church at Philippi in Macedonia, which he had founded around AD 49 (Acts 16). Written from prison, it thanks the Philippians for a gift, tells them his news, urges them to unity and humility after the example of Christ, warns against those who insisted on circumcision, and is full of joy. It contains the great passage on Christ’s humbling and exaltation (2:5–11) and the promise of God’s peace that is beyond all our understanding (4:6–7).

qa.question: Who wrote Philippians, and where was Paul when he wrote it?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, writing with Timothy (1:1). Almost all scholars agree the letter is his. He was in chains (1:13) and sent greetings from those in the emperor’s household (4:22). The traditional view, still the most widely held, is that he wrote from house arrest in Rome around AD 60–62; some scholars prefer an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus, around AD 54–55, and others Caesarea. Some also think the letter combines two or three shorter notes, though many defend it as a single letter.

qa.question: What does it mean that Christ “emptied himself” in Philippians 2:7?
qa.answer: Paul says that Christ, being in the form of God, did not treat equality with God as something to exploit for himself, but emptied himself by taking on the form of a servant and becoming human, and humbled himself to death on a cross; so God exalted him and gave him the name above every name. The church has always held that the Son did not stop being God. He emptied himself by taking on what he was not, not by giving up what he was. Paul tells the story so that believers will think the same way toward one another (2:5).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
